chunks: Microcontroller vs microprocessor. The question: What is the difference between a microcontroller and a microprocessor?
A microcontroller (MCU) is a whole small computer on one chip: processor, program storage, working memory and input/output hardware.
A microprocessor (MPU) is mostly the processor. It needs separate memory and storage chips and usually runs a full operating system. The trade is simple.
The MCU is cheap, frugal and predictable. The MPU is far more powerful but costs more, uses more power and is harder to design with.
An MCU is like a pocket calculator. Switch it on and it works at once, and it takes the same time to do the same job every time. An MPU is like a laptop.
It has much more power, but it needs memory and storage installed, takes a while to start, and how fast it answers depends on whatever else is running.
The MCU system is a chip, a regulator and a crystal.
The MPU system is the processor surrounded by DRAM, boot storage and a power-management IC, each of which needs its own routing and layout.
Microcontroller (MCU): processor, memory and input/output blocks together on one chip ("Common microcontrollers and microprocessors").
Microprocessor (MPU): a processor that relies on external memory and storage.
Operating system (OS): the software layer, such as Linux, that runs and shares the hardware among many programs. Deterministic: the same job takes the same time on every run.
Interrupt: a hardware signal that makes the processor drop its work and handle an event right now. Boot time: how long the chip takes to start doing useful work after power-on.
A typical small MCU (an Arm Cortex-M) starts handling an interrupt in about 12 clock ticks.
At 48 megahertz (48 million ticks per second) that is 12 / 48 million = 250 nanoseconds (billionths of a second), every time.
A Linux MPU might handle the same event in microseconds on one run and milliseconds on the next. The MCU also wakes in milliseconds and can sleep on millionths of an amp.
So a battery door lock uses an MCU, while a video doorbell uses an MPU. That is the whole idea.
"A microcontroller integrates the CPU, flash, SRAM and peripherals on one chip, so it runs on its own: low cost, microamp sleep, millisecond boot, deterministic timing, bare-metal or an RTOS.

A microprocessor is mainly the CPU and relies on external DRAM, storage and a PMIC; it's faster and runs Linux with an MMU, but costs more, draws watts, needs a complex board, and has non-deterministic timing.
Use an MCU for control and low power, an MPU for rich software, and often both together."
